props.title: Life, Above All
props.initialSlug: Young girl fights AIDS stigma in South African town

sections.content: **Life, Above All** (2010) stands as a powerful South African drama that confronts HIV/AIDS stigma through the eyes of 12-year-old Chanda. Director Oliver Schmitz crafts a devastating portrait of community prejudice that recalls the raw emotional impact of Yesterday (2004) and the child's perspective storytelling of Tsotsi (2005). The film's unflinching look at how AIDS affects families and communities in South Africa builds on earlier African cinema like Beat the Drum (2003), but brings a fresh urgency through its focus on a young girl fighting to protect her mother's dignity.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its young protagonist Khomotso Manyaka, whose performance as Chanda echoes other remarkable child performances in African cinema like War Witch (2012) and **Lamb** (2015). Through her eyes, we witness how whispers and rumors can destroy families, while also seeing the resilience of children forced to become adults too soon. The way Schmitz handles these heavy themes without exploitation recalls **In a Better World** (2010).

What sets **Life, Above All** apart is its intimate portrayal of mother-daughter relationships under extreme duress. Like **The First Grader** (2010) and **A Screaming Man** (2010), the film uses personal stories to illuminate larger social issues. The cinematography by Bernhard Jasper captures both the sun-baked beauty of the South African township and the dark corners where prejudice festers. SUBHEAD: African Cinema's Evolution

sections.content: **Life, Above All** represents a crucial moment in contemporary African cinema, building on foundations laid by films like **Moolaadé** (2004) and **Bamako** (2006). Its production quality and international reach helped pave the way for later successes like **Queen of Katwe** (2016) and **I Am Not a Witch** (2017), showing how African stories can resonate globally while maintaining cultural authenticity.
